mcqs.question: After rebasing a feature branch onto main, why do all of the feature branch's commits end up with new hashes?
options: Because git recreates each commit with a new parent, and a commit's hash is derived from its content including its parent
Because rebase re-hashes commits as a side effect of updating the branch pointer
Because the commit messages are automatically rewritten during a rebase
Only commits that had a conflict get a new hash; the rest are untouched
mcqs.explanation: A commit's hash is computed over its content, including a reference to its parent commit — change the parent and the hash necessarily changes, even if the diff and message are identical. It isn't a side effect of moving a pointer, messages aren't rewritten by default, and every replayed commit gets a new hash, not just the ones with conflicts.

mcqs.question: What is the golden rule that determines whether it's safe to rebase a branch?
options: Only rebase branches with fewer than ten commits
Never rebase commits that other people have already fetched or built work on top of
Only rebase feature branches, never bugfix branches
Always rebase before merging, regardless of who else has the branch
mcqs.explanation: The risk is entirely about whether someone else already has a copy of the commits you're about to rewrite — rebase creates new hashes, so anyone with the old ones ends up with a diverged, confusing history. It has nothing to do with commit count or branch naming, and rebasing unconditionally before every merge ignores exactly this risk.

mcqs.question: A team wants every commit on main to be independently buildable so `git bisect` can pinpoint regressions cleanly. Which approach best supports that?
options: Merge commits, since they clearly mark where each feature was integrated
Whichever approach produces the most commits, since bisect works better with more data points
Rebasing feature branches before landing them, since each resulting commit is a clean, linear step with no merge commit obscuring which side introduced a change
It doesn't matter — bisect works identically regardless of history shape
mcqs.explanation: A linear, rebased history gives bisect a clean sequence of individually buildable commits to search through; merge commits can hide which parent's changes introduced a regression, making bisect's job harder. More commits alone doesn't help, and history shape does materially affect how useful bisect is.

mcqs.question: You rebase a shared branch locally and need to push the result. Why does `git push --force-with-lease` protect against the worst outcome that a plain `git push --force` doesn't?
options: It automatically resolves any conflicts with the remote branch
It refuses to push if the remote has changed since you last fetched, instead of overwriting it unconditionally
It creates a backup branch on the remote before pushing
It only pushes commits that don't already exist on the remote
mcqs.explanation: force-with-lease checks that the remote tip still matches what you last saw before overwriting it, so it fails loudly if a teammate pushed in the meantime — plain force overwrites regardless. It doesn't resolve conflicts, create backups, or filter which commits get pushed.

mcqs.question: How does `git pull --rebase` differ from a plain `git pull` when your local branch has unpushed commits?
options: It fetches and replays your local commits on top of the updated remote tip instead of creating a merge commit
It discards your local commits and replaces them with the remote's version
It behaves identically to a plain pull but skips the fetch step
It only works if there are no new commits on the remote at all
mcqs.explanation: A plain pull merges, producing a merge commit when both sides have diverged; --rebase instead replays your local commits on top of the freshly fetched tip, keeping history linear. It doesn't discard anything, still does a real fetch, and works precisely in the case where the remote has new commits.
